previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted for worsening rectal prolapse with associated fecal incontinence, rectal bleeding, and recent weight gain. She underwent a perineal rectosigmoidectomy with levatorplasty the following day. Post-operatively, she developed a transient post-operative ileus with abdominal distension, managed conservatively without a nasogastric tube. She had low urine output initially, which resolved with IV fluids and restart of home diuretics. A urinalysis before discharge revealed a urinary tract infection, and she was started on ciprofloxacin. Her diet was advanced as bowel function returned, and she passed a bowel movement on hospital day 6. She recovered well, with stable chronic diastolic heart failure and no surgical complications. She was discharged home with services on day 8 with instructions for bowel management, activity restrictions, and follow-up.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Recent surgery, white blood cell count, rectal bleeding.

TECHNIQUE:  Frontal and lateral views of the chest.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

The patient is status post median sternotomy.  The patient is rotated somewhat
to the left.  There is right mid and low to lower lung atelectasis.  Patchy
opacities in the left lower lobe could be due to atelectasis although
aspiration or pneumonia is not excluded.  Multiple old right-sided rib
deformities are again seen.  The aorta is tortuous.  The cardiac silhouette is
top-normal.  No large pleural effusion or pneumothorax is seen.  There may be
a hiatal hernia.  Surgical clips are seen projecting over the right axilla.

IMPRESSION:

Right basilar atelectasis.  Patchy left base opacity may be due to atelectasis
although underlying consolidation due to infection or aspiration not excluded.

INDICATION:  History of rectal prolapse surgery, presenting with bilateral
lower quadrant abdominal pain and rectal bleeding.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the lung bases to the lesser
trochanter after the administration of oral contrast.  Coronal and sagittal
reformations were prepared.  DLP:  678.17 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis, ___.

CT ABDOMEN:  There is bibasilar atelectasis.  The visualized portions of the
heart and pericardium are noteworthy for coronary artery calcifications.  The
patient has had a prior fundoplication.  Oral contrast passes through the
stomach and small bowel into the ascending colon without evidence of
obstruction.  Evaluation of the liver is limited in the absence of intravenous
contrast, but there is no gross abnormality.  The pancreas is atrophic and
contains a 1.9 x 1.7 cm hypodense cystic lesion in the uncinate process,
similar to prior imaging (2:32).

The right kidney is atrophic.  There is no hydronephrosis in the left kidney. 
11-mm hypodensity on the left is probably a simple cyst (2:22).  The spleen is
normal.  The gallbladder wall is mildly thickened, but not distended.  There
is no free intraperitoneal air.  

Eccentric positioning of the atherosclerotic plaques in the abdominal aorta
have been present for multiple priors and consistent with an old dissection
(2:21).

CT PELVIS:  There is a large fluid collection anterior to the rectosigmoid
colon measuring 8.5 x 7.0 cm and containing nondependent locules of air.  The
colon passes along this finding and oral contrast has not reached this point
to exclude a leak.  There is also an apparent tract from the rectum to this
collection (602B:31).  The colon proximal to this is unremarkable.  The
urinary bladder is unremarkable.  The uterus is absent.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There are multilevel degenerative changes at the
thoracolumbar spine including anterior wedging of T11-T12.  There is no lytic
or blastic lesion worrisome for malignancy.

IMPRESSION:
1.  8.5-cm perirectal fluid collection concerning for abscess and anastomotic
leak.  Gastrografin enema can be considered if confirmation is needed.
2.  Chronic dissection of the abdominal aorta with atrophy of the right
kidney.
3.  Nonspecific gallbladder wall edema.  No distention or specific signs of
acute cholecystitis.
4.  Stable cystic pancreatic lesion described as probable on IPMN on prior MR.
___ follow-up with MRCP is recommended.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with perirectal fluid collection likely from
anastomotic leak.  For CT-guided drainage.  

COMPARISON:  Recent unenhanced CT scan from ___. 

OPERATORS: Dr. ___, radiology attending and Dr ___, abdominal imaging
fellow. 

Dr. ___ was present in the CT procedural suite throughout the procedure.  

FINDINGS:

A limited prone low-dose CT scan performed through pelvis to plan the
procedure.  Following review of the images, a right perirectal collection was
identified, however it was difficult to discern the rectum from the
collection.  A Foley catheter was inserted into the rectum and dilute barium
was instilled to opacify the rectum. 

PROCEDURE:

After informed consent was signed by the patient, the patient was taken to the
CT procedure suite and placed in a prone position. The time out procedure was
performed per ___ protocol. An entrance site was determined for aspiration
and drainage of right pelvic collection via a right trans gluteal approach.
The patient was prepped and draped in usual sterile fashion. 1% lidocaine was
used for local anesthesia in the right gluteal region. 

Using CT guidance, an 18 gauge ___ needle was advanced into the right
pelvic fluid collection, confirmed by aspiration of 1 cc of thick
serosanguineous fluid.  Using Seldinger technique, using ___ wires, 6 and
7 ___ dilators, a 8 ___ ___ catheter was advanced into the right
pelvic collection.  Approximately 16 cc of thick serosanguineous fluid was
aspirated.

The aspirate was sent for microbiology evaluation.  The catheter were attached
to suction bulb.  The catheter was secured with adhesive gauze.  No
periprocedural complications were encountered.  The patient tolerated the
procedure well and was transferred to the medical unit in stable condition. 

Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of fentanyl (150
mcg) throughout the total intra service time of 60 min during which the
patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored. 

IMPRESSION:

Successful drainage of right pelvic fluid collection using 8 ___ ___
catheters.  Approximately 16 cc of thick serosanguineous fluid aspirated.  No
periprocedural complications.

INDICATION:  Female with rectal prolapse status post perineal
rectosigmoidectomy with levatorplasty complicated by anastomotic leak.  The
anastomosis is low.  Anastomotic leak drained by ___ ___.

COMPARISON: CT abdomen and pelvis ___ and ___

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous helical MDCT images were obtained through the pelvis
without IV after the administration of rectal contrast by rectal tube.  In
addition, a delayed sequence was obtained after removal of the rectal tube. 
Multiplanar axial, coronal, and sagittal images were generated.

TOTAL BODY DLP:  1218.1 mGy-cm

CT PELVIS WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:  The patient is status post rectosigmoidectomy
with low anastomosis.  There is opacification of bowel to about the proximal
sigmoid. Opacification of the remaining partially imaged portions of large
bowel may reflect retained contrast from prior CT. 

A percutaneous pelvic drain is in the right hemipelvis (4:22).  Prior 8.5 cm
perirectal fluid collection is significantly decreased in size with only
minimal residual fluid (4:24) and fat stranding.  There are a few locules of
gas tracking from the anastamosis superiorly (4:35, 30 and 19) and leakage of
contrast  posteriorly into the residual collection (13:39 and 9:23).  

The remaining included loops of small and large bowel are unremarkable with
the exception of scattered sigmoid diverticula. There is no pelvic wall or
inguinal lymphadenopathy.

The bladder is normal.  No uterus is likely surgically absent.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Significant decrease in pelvic fluid collection with minimal fluid
remaining.

2.  Gas in the pelvis and leak of rectal contrast into the collection at the
anastomosis compatible with persistent anastomotic leak.

PROCEDURE:
The procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives were explained to the
patient and after a detailed discussion, informed written consent was obtained
by Dr. ___.  A preprocedure timeout using three patient identifiers was
performed as per ___ protocol.

The patient was placed in a prone position on the CT scan table and a
preprocedure non-contrast CT of the pelvis redemonstrated the right
transgluteal drainage catheter in satisfactory position, with only minimal
residual amount of fluid within the pelvis.  Contrast noted within the colon,
likely from previous contrast study.  Low rectosigmoid anastomosis is again
noted, similar to previous.  Moderate atherosclerosis of the visualized
vessels.

The patient was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  5 cc of 1%
lidocaine were administered to the subcutaneous tissues for local anesthetic
effect.  Under CT guidance, the existing pigtail catheter was cut and a 0.35
___ wire was introduced through the catheter into the pelvic collection
and exchange was made for a new 8 ___ pigtail ___ catheter.  The
position of the drain was confirmed with a repeat non-contrast pelvic CT
demonstrating satisfactory position of the pigtail catheter within the pelvis.
The pigtail was formed and attached to a JP suction bulb for drainage.  The
pigtail catheter was fixed in place with a StatLock.  There were no immediate
post-procedural complications and the patient tolerated the procedure well.  A
total of 0.5 mg of Versed were given to the patient for sedation by an
independent trained radiology nursing throughout which the patient's
hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored, although this did not
qualify as moderate sedation.

The attending radiologist, Dr. ___, was present throughout the
entire duration of the procedure.

IMPRESSION:
Technically successful CT-guided catheter exchange of right transgluteal
pigtail catheter.  No immediate post-procedural complications.
